ATHENS, Greece (CNN) -- Authorities vowed to re-impose order after demonstrators rose up across Greece Monday in a third day of rioting over Saturday's killing of a 15-year-old boy that has left dozens injured and scores of properties destroyed. An undated photo of Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose death has sparked riots across Greece. "Under no circumstances will the government accept what is occurring," said Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos. "We will do what is necessary." It was unclear what would be necessary to placate the demonstrators. "We've just lost count of how many demonstrations are taking place now," a police spokesman in Athens told CNN. Police said 34 civilians and 16 police officers were injured Monday in rioting that spread into new municipalities, including Trikala, Larissam and Veria. Riots broke out Saturday in Thessaloniki and Athens, where police killed the teen.  Watch the latest report on the rioting » . Demonstrators had torched three government buildings and three offices of the ruling conservative political party in downtown Athens, a National Fire Brigade spokesman told Greek state television. Watch as iReporter witnesses the clashes . Thirty-five cars and 160 trash containers also had been set ablaze, he said.  See images of anarchy on Greek streets » . Demonstrators Monday barricaded streets in Athens and Thessaloniki and hurled gasoline bombs as they battled with police. Clouds of tear gas hung over the capital city as riot police continued to battle the hundreds of young self-styled anarchists rioting over the boy's death. "Rage is what I feel for what has happened, rage, and that this cop who did it must see what it is to kill a kid and to destroy a life," a student in Athens told reporters Monday.  Watch protesters clash with police » . In a nationally televised address broadcast on state television, Greek Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence and promised to punish those responsible for Saturday's shooting. He also announced a decision to drop plans to reimburse business owners affected by the rioting. The police officer who fired the fatal shot has been charged with "manslaughter with intent" and suspended from duty, police said, adding that a second police officer was arrested Saturday on criminal accessory charges. Government officials have condemned the shooting. "An investigation is under way and those found responsible will be punished," said Pavlopoulos. "Measures will also be taken to avoid such incidents again in the future." iReport.com: Are you there? Share photos, video of rioting . On Monday, authorities conducted an autopsy on the teenage boy in an effort to answer questions about the circumstances of the shooting, but the boy's family has called in their own investigators to verify state findings, the Athens coroner told CNN. The U.S. and British embassies issued warnings to employees and tourists on Sunday, instructing them to avoid downtown Athens and other major cities until rioting subsides. Tourists in central Athens hotels were advised by hotel staff not to leave their rooms as police fanned out across the city. "There are lots of burning bins and debris in the street and a huge amount of tear gas in the air, which we got choked with on the way back to our hotel," according to Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer visiting Athens on Sunday. A police statement about the teenage boy's death said the incident started when six young protesters pelted a police patrol car with stones. The teen was shot as he tried to throw a petrol bomb at the officers, police said. Other angry teens converged on the site almost immediately. Fighting between youths and police erupted elsewhere, including Thessaloniki, the country's second-largest city. Hundreds of young people took to the streets of the sprawling port city, finally barricading themselves behind the gates of a state university. Authorities have been barred from entering university grounds since tanks crushed a 1973 student uprising protesting the ruling military junta. It was not clear what authorities would do about the demonstrators still holed up at the university. No deaths have been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 protesters had been rounded up for questioning. Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.

**Tragedy Triggers Turmoil: Greece Plunged into Chaos Following Fatal Police Shooting of Teenager**

What began as a tragic Saturday night confrontation in the heart of Athens rapidly escalated into one of the most severe civil crises in Greece’s modern history. The fatal police shooting of a 15-year-old boy acted as a spark in a powder keg, igniting a wave of violent riots that quickly paralyzed major cities across the country, leaving a trail of destruction, dozens of injuries, and a nation grappling with deep political and social fractures.

The deadly incident occurred in Exarcheia, a central Athens neighborhood known for its historic ties to radical political movements and frequent friction with law enforcement. According to witness accounts, an altercation broke out between a small group of youths and a police patrol. Within moments, a officer drew his service weapon and fired, striking the teenager in the chest. News of the boy’s death spread instantly across social media and news outlets, transforming raw grief into immediate, fiery indignation. 

By midnight, the capital had descended into violent unrest. Thousands of demonstrators, ranging from high school students and university activists to self-described anarchists, poured into the streets. Protesters constructed makeshift barricades out of overturned vehicles, burning trash dumpsters, and torn-up street pavement. Armed with Molotov cocktails, stones, and flare guns, violent factions launched sustained attacks against police lines, government buildings, and symbolic targets of commercial wealth. 

Law enforcement responded aggressively, deploying heavy barrages of tear gas and flash-bang grenades in an effort to disperse the crowds. A choking blanket of chemical smoke hung over central Athens as riot police engaged in intense, street-by-street battles with masked protesters. 

The chaos was not contained to the capital. Within hours, the unrest swept across the nation like wildfire. In Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, protesters attacked administrative offices and burned police vehicles. Similar clashes erupted in Patras, Ioannina, and on the islands of Crete and Corfu. High-street commercial districts became war zones: luxury boutiques were looted, corporate bank branches were firebombed, and dozens of private vehicles were reduced to charred metal hulls. Emergency services struggled to respond as firefighters faced attacks while trying to douse blazes burning throughout city centers.

Hospitals reported treating dozens of people for severe smoke inhalation, burn injuries, fractures, and trauma caused by flying debris, including both riot police officers and civilian demonstrators.

Faced with a rapidly deteriorating situation, top Greek officials were forced into crisis management. The Prime Minister delivered a solemn, televised address to the nation, forcefully condemning the violence while expressing deep sorrow over the youth's tragic death. He vowed that a rigorous and transparent investigation into the officer's actions would take place, promising that "zero tolerance" would be applied and that those responsible for the shooting would face strict legal accountability. Simultaneously, government ministers sternly warned that the state would take all necessary measures to restore law and order, appealing for calm as economic leaders warned of the catastrophic financial impact of the destruction.

Despite official pleas for restraint, the violence represents far more than a reaction to a single tragic event. Analysts point out that the shooting struck a nerve in a society already burdened by economic uncertainty, high youth unemployment, and a deep-seated distrust of state authority. As smoke continues to rise from burnt-out storefronts, Greece finds itself at a dangerous crossroads, facing a protracted national crisis that has shattered public trust and left the country's cities severely scarred.

**Athens: The Timeless Capital Modernized for the Global Stage**

Athens, the vibrant capital of Greece, is a city where the echoes of antiquity seamlessly blend with the energy of contemporary urban life. Long celebrated as the cradle of Western civilization and the birthplace of democracy, this Mediterranean metropolis is currently experiencing a dynamic cultural and economic renaissance—one that has captured the attention of major global media outlets, including CNN.

For decades, international travelers viewed Athens primarily as a temporary stopover—a brief pause to see the iconic Parthenon atop the Acropolis before rushing off to the sun-drenched Greek islands. Today, that narrative has shifted dramatically. In numerous feature stories and travel guides, CNN has highlighted Athens as a world-class destination in its own right, praising its bustling neighborhood culture, world-class gastronomy, and thriving arts scene.

Step onto the streets of Athens, and the contrast between old and new is striking. Beneath the shadow of 2,500-year-old marble temples, neighborhoods like Koukaki, Pangrati, and Psirri thrum with new energy. Traditional *tavernas* serving classic Greek dishes now sit alongside innovative, Michelin-starred restaurants and trendy third-wave coffee shops. As CNN Travel has frequently noted, the city's rooftop bars offer some of the most spectacular nightlife views in Europe, allowing patrons to sip craft cocktails while gazing at the illuminated Acropolis.

Beyond its historical allure and culinary delights, Athens reflects the resilient spirit of modern Greece. Following a challenging economic decade, the city has reinvented itself through local creativity, tech innovation, and sustainable urban developments like the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center and the ambitious Ellinikon project along the Athenian Riviera. 

Whether CNN is reporting on Greece's surging tourism numbers, the transformation of its coastal districts, or its booming digital nomad scene, Athens remains at the center of the story. It is a city that honors its monumental past while boldly shaping its future, offering every visitor an unforgettable taste of Greek *filoxenia* (hospitality) in a captivating modern setting.

### Key Coverage Summary: Day 3 of the Athens Riots (December 8, 2008)

#### Background of the Escalation
On Saturday, December 6, 2008, 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos was fatally shot by a police officer in the Exarcheia neighborhood of central Athens. The shooting immediately sparked intense clashes between police, students, and anarchist groups, which escalated over the weekend and culminated in massive violent demonstrations on Monday, December 8.

#### Main Developments Reported on Day 3

1. **Widespread Violence in Central Athens:**
   * Riots spread heavily across central Athens, particularly around Syntagma Square, Omonoia Square, and outside the Hellenic Parliament building.
   * Protesters threw Molotov cocktails, stones, and debris at riot police, who responded with extensive use of tear gas, turning downtown streets into smoke-filled conflict zones.
   * Dozens of luxury shops, department stores, bank branches, and car dealerships were vandalized or set on fire along major commercial avenues such as Ermou Street.

2. **Spread to Other Greek Cities:**
   * Violence was not contained to the capital; major clashes were reported in Thessaloniki (Greece's second-largest city), Patras, Corfu, and several locations on the island of Crete.
   * Protesters attacked police stations and local government buildings across the country.

3. **Government Reaction and Political Crisis:**
   * Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis held emergency meetings with his cabinet and senior security officials to address the crisis.
   * In a televised address, Karamanlis strongly condemned the police shooting as an unacceptable act, promising a full and transparent investigation. He simultaneously called for calm, stating that the violence and destruction of public and private property would not be tolerated.
   * Opposition parties heavily criticized the government’s handling of both police oversight and the public security response.

4. **Legal Action Against the Police Officers:**
   * News reports confirmed that two police officers involved in the incident were arrested. 
   * The officer who fired the shot, Epaminondas Korkoneas, was charged with intentional homicide (and later convicted), while his partner was charged as an accomplice.
   * Initial police statements claimed the officer fired warning shots after being attacked by a group of youths, but eyewitness reports and preliminary investigations disputed this narrative.

5. **Broader Socioeconomic Context:**
   * Reports highlighted that the anger behind the riots extended beyond the immediate tragedy of the shooting. 
   * The unrest tapped into deep-seated frustration among Greek youth over high youth unemployment, economic instability, government corruption, and police brutality—setting the stage for the broader social turbulence during the impending Greek financial crisis.

6. **Impact on Infrastructure and Education:**
   * Dozens of university campuses, high schools, and public buildings were occupied by students and activists.
   * Public transit in Athens faced severe disruptions, and international travel warnings were issued by several foreign embassies as downtown violence destabilized routine public life.

**ATHENS IN FLAMES: Greece Gripped by Unprecedented Civil Unrest After Police Kill Teenager**

**By CNN Staff**
**Updated 11:45 PM EST, Wednesday, December 10, 2008**
**Location: ATHENS, Greece**

**(CNN)** — Plumes of acrid black smoke hang low over the historic center of Athens tonight, obscuring the ancient Parthenon as Greece descends into its worst civil unrest in more than a generation. 

What began as a localized outburst of rage over the fatal police shooting of a 15-year-old boy on Saturday night has erupted into a nationwide uprising. Cities across the country—from Thessaloniki in the north to the island of Crete in the south—are suffering nightly scenes of urban warfare, paralyzing the nation, shattering its economy, and pushing the conservative government of Prime Minister Costas Karamanlis to the brink of collapse.

### The Spark: A Fatal Encounter in Exarcheia

The catalyst for the violence occurred late Saturday evening, December 6, in Exarcheia, a central Athens neighborhood historically associated with radical political movements and student counter-culture. 

According to police accounts, a squad car carrying two officers was pelted with stones and bottles by a group of youths. Police say one officer fired three shots—claiming two were warning shots into the air and one ricocheted. Eyewitnesses, however, violently dispute that narrative, telling local media that the officer aimed directly at the group.

One bullet struck 15-year-old high school student Alexandros Grigoropoulos directly in the chest. He died before reaching the hospital.

Within hours, word of Grigoropoulos’s death detonated across social media and student networks. By midnight, central Athens was a furnace of rage.

### "Cold-Blooded Murder" vs. State Apologies

The outrage was immediate and unforgiving. The victim’s family has publicly rejected initial police claims that the officers acted in self-defense. 

"This was not an accident. It was a cold-blooded murder of a child," said Alexis Kougias, the defense attorney representing the suspect officer, in a statement outlining the family's view of the tragedy. "Alexandros was simply hanging out with friends. He posed no threat to anyone."

The officer who fired the fatal shot, 37-year-old Epaminondas Korkoneas, has been charged with intentional homicide and remains in custody alongside his partner, Vassilis Saraliotis, who is charged as an accomplice. 

Facing a mounting political catastrophe, Prime Minister Costas Karamanlis delivered a televised national address in a bid to restore calm. 

"I express my deep sorrow, as a Prime Minister, as a citizen, and as a father, for the death of young Alexandros," Karamanlis said, his tone solemn. "No one has the right to use this tragic event as an excuse for actions of violence against innocent people, against society, and against democracy itself. The culprits will be punished strictly and uncompromisingly."

Despite the Prime Minister's plea for composure, opposition leaders have openly criticized the administration's handling of the security crisis. George Papandreou, leader of the opposition PASOK party, declared: "The government has lost the trust of the Greek people. They can no longer guarantee safety, order, or economic stability."

### Millions in Damage: A Trail of Destruction

The economic toll of the riots is staggering. What started as student demonstrations quickly expanded to include anarchists, labor unions, and disenfranchised citizens angry over rising poverty and youth unemployment.

According to data released Wednesday by the Athens Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI):

* **Damaged Businesses:** More than **435 shops and storefronts** have been heavily damaged, burned, or looted in central Athens alone.
* **Financial Impact:** Initial commercial losses in the capital are estimated to exceed **€50 million ($65 million USD)**, not including public infrastructure damages.
* **Banking Sector:** Over **50 bank branches** have been firebombed or vandalized.
* **Casualties and Arrests:** The Ministry of Public Order reports that over **70 police officers** and dozens of civilians have been hospitalized with injuries ranging from severe burns to smoke inhalation. More than **200 people have been arrested or detained** nationwide.
* **Infrastructure:** Dozens of municipal buses, private vehicles, and university buildings—including the historic National Technical University of Athens—have been gutted by fire.

In Syntagma Square, the heart of commercial and political life in Athens, the city's official 40-foot Christmas tree was set ablaze by rioters wielding Molotov cocktails—a striking symbol of the breakdown in order.

### A Generation's Boiling Point

While the death of Alexandros Grigoropoulos was the catalyst, political analysts insist the underlying fuel for the riots has been building for years. Greece is grappling with deep-seated corruption, a looming debt crisis, and a staggering youth unemployment rate that hovers near 25%. 

The young protesters have coined a phrase for themselves: "The €700 Generation"—referring to the average maximum monthly salary a university graduate can expect in an increasingly stagnant economy.

"This isn't just about police brutality anymore," said Elena Theodorou, a 22-year-old sociology student protesting outside Parliament. "We have no future. They kill our children, they steal our money, and they leave us with nothing. Alexandros was one of us."

Furthermore, anti-police sentiment runs deep in Greek culture, stemming from the brutal military junta that ruled the country from 1967 to 1974. Under Greek law, police are traditionally banned from entering university campuses—a legacy designed to protect political speech, but one that has allowed campuses to become safe havens for rioters manufacturing petrol bombs.

### The World Watches as Chaos Spreads

The violence is no longer confined to Greek borders. Solidarity protests, some turning violent, have been reported outside Greek embassies in London, Berlin, Paris, and Rome.

In Greece, a 24-hour general strike called by labor unions on Wednesday paralyzed public transport, grounded flights, and shut down government offices, adding to the sense that the nation is grinding to a complete halt.

As night falls once again over Athens, helmeted riot police armed with tear gas and stun grenades line the perimeter of Parliament. Across the street, hundreds of masked youths clad in black are assembling behind improvised barricades made of overturned dumpsters and smashed marble. 

With Alexandros Grigoropoulos set to be buried later this week, authorities fear the worst of the violence may still be to come.

*Reporting live from Athens, Nicole Johnston, CNN.*

In December 2008, CNN—along with other major international news outlets—provided extensive, ongoing coverage of the violent riots that erupted across Greece following the fatal police shooting of **15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos** in Athens. 

Below is an overview of how CNN reported on the 2008 Greek riots, the key themes of their coverage, and the context provided at the time.

---

### 1. The Catalyst (December 6, 2008)
CNN reported that on the evening of December 6, 2008, Alexandros Grigoropoulos was shot dead by a police officer, Epaminondas Korkoneas, in the Exarcheia district of Athens—an area historically associated with radical left-wing and anarchist movements. 
* **CNN's Framing:** Early reports focused on the immediate conflict of narratives. The police initially claimed the officer fired warning shots that ricocheted, while eyewitnesses told reporters (and posted videos online) that the officer aimed directly at the teenager.
* CNN highlighted the rapid spread of news via early social media platforms, blogs, and text messaging, which mobilized thousands of high school and university students within hours.

---

### 2. Main Themes in CNN’s Coverage

#### A. "Athens in Flames" and Visual Impact
CNN’s live broadcasts and digital reports heavily emphasized the scale of destruction in central Athens, particularly around Syntagma Square, the Greek Parliament, and Panepistimiou Street. 
* Reports detailed heavy clashes using **petrol bombs (Molotov cocktails), rocks, and tear gas**.
* Images of burning Christmas trees in front of Parliament, destroyed banks, storefronts, and overturned cars were central to CNN’s prime-time coverage.
* CNN reported that the violence quickly spread beyond Athens to Thessaloniki, Crete, Corfu, and Patras, turning into nationwide unrest.

#### B. The "Generation of 700 Euros" (Economic & Social Undercurrents)
While the immediate cause was police brutality, CNN's international correspondents (such as Christiane Amanpour and regional reporters) delved deeper into the socio-economic causes.
* CNN framed the riots as an explosion of anger from a **disillusioned youth population**. 
* They highlighted the term *"Generation of 700 Euros"*—referring to educated young Greeks who faced high unemployment, low wages, temporary jobs, and lack of opportunity.
* Network analysts pointed out that the shooting acted as a spark for frustration that had been building against systemic political corruption and economic stagnation, serving as a harbinger for the major Greek debt crisis that officially erupted a year later (2009–2010).

#### C. Political Turmoil and Government Vulnerability
CNN monitored the political fallout closely, focusing on the fragile Conservative government of Prime Minister **Kostas Karamanlis**.
* Reports stressed that the government was caught off-guard and appeared powerless to stop the destruction, torn between using heavy police force (which risked escalating public anger) or taking a passive stance (which angered business owners).
* CNN covered the general strikes called by trade unions (GSEE and ADEDY) during the riots, which paralyzed public transport, airports, and public services, compounding the crisis.

---

### 3. Chronological Arc of CNN's Reporting (Dec 2008)

* **Days 1–3 (Dec 6–8):** Focus on the shooting, immediate night of rage, arresting of the involved officers, and the initial wave of global shock.
* **Days 4–7 (Dec 9–12):** Coverage of Grigoropoulos’s funeral (attended by thousands in Paleio Faliro), which was marked by tear gas and clashes nearby. Reports emphasized solidarity protests spreading to European cities like London, Paris, and Berlin.
* **Mid-to-Late December:** Shift toward assessing the economic damage (estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros) and discussing long-term political instability in Greece.

---

### 4. Legacy in International Media
CNN's coverage of the 2008 Greek riots marked a turning point in how international media viewed Greece. Rather than seeing it merely as a Mediterranean holiday destination or a stable EU member state, CNN framed the 2008 events as the **first violent tremor of Europe's post-2008 economic destabilization**. 

Every year since, CNN and international media monitor December 6th in Athens, as annual anniversary marches in memory of Alexandros Grigoropoulos frequently lead to renewed clashes between demonstrators and police.

counterfactuals.prompt: You are an international news correspondent in December 2008. Write a comprehensive news report from Athens detailing the third straight day of youth riots, covering police responses, government statements, and historical context like the 1973 university sanctuary law.
counterfactuals.output:
**DATELINE: ATHENS, Greece — Monday, December 8, 2008**

A thick, acrid haze of tear gas and burning rubber hangs heavy over the center of Athens tonight, choking the broad avenues around Syntagma Square as Greece endures its third consecutive day of fierce youth violence. What began on Saturday night as spontaneous rage over the police killing of a 15-year-old boy has rapidly transformed into the worst domestic civil unrest this Mediterranean nation has witnessed in decades.

From the northern port city of Thessaloniki to the southern island of Crete, urban centers across the country have descended into chaos. Here in the capital, the scene resembles a war zone: barricades built from overturned dumpsters crackle with fire, luxury storefronts lay shattered, and the grand festive Christmas tree standing outside the Hellenic Parliament was reduced to ash earlier this evening by youth hurling petrol bombs.

The catalyst for this nationwide explosion of fury occurred late Saturday evening in Exarcheia, a bohemian, fiercely anti-establishment neighborhood in central Athens. According to eyewitnesses, 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos was out with friends when a violent altercation broke out between a group of teenagers and a police patrol. Minutes later, two shots rang out. Grigoropoulos was struck in the chest and died before reaching the hospital.

### A Government on the Defensive

Speaking in a televised address to a panicked nation late Sunday, conservative Prime Minister Costas Karamanlis expressed deep sorrow over the youth's death, describing it as an "unpardonable tragedy." 

"I know that nothing can heal the pain of a child lost," Karamanlis said, his voice visibly strained. "The state will guarantee a transparent investigation, and those responsible will be punished severely. But I ask for calm. Violence cannot be tolerated."

Authorities moved swiftly to detain the two officers involved. The officer who fired the fatal shot, 37-year-old Epaminondas Korkoneas, has been arrested and charged with intentional homicide, while his partner faces charges as an accomplice. Defense lawyers for Korkoneas claim the officer fired warning shots into the air and ground, and that the fatal bullet ricocheted. However, ballistics reports remain pending, and public fury shows no signs of abating.

Despite the government's pleas for restraint, the police response on the ground has done little to soothe public anger. Riot police clad in full armor, wielding shields and batons, have fired thousands of rounds of tear gas into crowd formations, turning the marble walkways of central Athens into slippery, tear-soaked battlegrounds. Human rights groups and opposition leaders have criticized the police for aggressive tactics, while shopkeepers—watching their livelihoods go up in flames—have slammed the security forces for failing to protect property.

### Shadows of 1973: Sanctuary and Deep-Seated Mistrust

To understand the velocity of this rage, one must look past the immediate trauma of Saturday night and examine Greece’s complex, turbulent history with state authority.

Much of the violent resistance is anchored around the National Technical University of Athens (the Athens Polytechnic). Under Greek law, universities benefit from a strict "academic sanctuary" principle—a direct legacy of the 1973 student uprising against the ruling military junta. In November 1973, tanks crashed through the gates of the Polytechnic to crush anti-dictatorship protests, killing dozens of civilians. 

When Greece restored democracy in 1974, lawmakers codified a law barring police and security forces from entering university campuses without the explicit permission of a university council composed of administrators and students. Today, young protesters use the sanctuary law to devastating tactical advantage: launching salvos of Molotov cocktails and stones at police lines, then retreating behind the gates of the Polytechnic, where police officers are legally powerless to pursue them.

### "The 700-Euro Generation"

While the memory of the junta fuels an institutional distrust of the police, commentators note that the raw fuel driving this weekend's riots is socio-economic despair. 

Greece’s youth are increasingly referred to as the *"700-Euro Generation"*—a cohort of highly educated young adults facing stagnant wages capped at €700 a month, soaring living costs, and an official youth unemployment rate hovering near 23 percent. Compounded by a global financial crisis that is beginning to hit Southern Europe, alongside a series of high-profile financial scandals plaguing the Karamanlis administration, a deep-seated hopelessness has taken root.

"This isn't just about Alexandros," said Nikos, a 22-year-old university student wearing a black scarf over his face near the barricades in Exarcheia. "Alexandros was one of us. The state doesn't give us a future, it doesn't give us jobs, and now its police shoot us in the street. We have nothing left to lose."

### An Uncertain Road Ahead

With a 24-hour general strike already scheduled for Wednesday by trade unions protesting government economic reforms, the government faces a grave crisis. As night falls once more over Athens, fire engines race through streets littered with smashed glass, spent tear-gas canisters, and anti-state graffiti reading: *"State of Murderers."*

With public anger showing no signs of cooling, and with university campuses firmly fortified by student activists, Greece prepares for another long, fraught night in a crisis that has pushed the nation to the brink.
